claim: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) symbioses contribute to global carbon cycles as plant hosts divert up to 20% of photosynthate to the obligate biotrophic fungi.
source: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) symbioses contribute to global carbon cycles as plant hosts divert up to 20% of photosynthate to the obligate biotrophic fungi.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of AM symbioses to carbon cycles, supported by established scientific knowledge about carbon allocation in these symbioses.

claim: Previous studies suggested carbohydrates as the only form of carbon transferred to AM fungi.
source: Previous studies suggested carbohydrates as the only form of carbon transferred to the fungi.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings, indicating it is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: De novo fatty acid (FA) synthesis has not been observed in AM fungi in absence of the plant.
source: However, de novo fatty acid (FA) synthesis has not been observed in AM fungi in absence of the plant.
evidence: This is a statement about observations from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Two Lotus japonicus mutants are defective in AM-specific paralogs of lipid biosynthesis genes (KASI and GPAT6).
source: In a forward genetic approach, we identified two Lotus japonicus mutants defective in AM-specific paralogs of lipid biosynthesis genes (KASI and GPAT6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the forward genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: The KASI and GPAT6 mutants perturb fungal development and accumulation of emblematic fungal 16:1ω5 FAs.
source: These mutants perturb fungal development and accumulation of emblematic fungal 16:1ω5 FAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 13C patterns of fungal FAs recapitulate those of wild-type hosts, indicating cross-kingdom lipid transfer from plants to fungi.
source: Using isotopolog profiling we demonstrate that 13C patterns of fungal FAs recapitulate those of wild-type hosts, indicating cross-kingdom lipid transfer from plants to fungi.
evidence: This claim is supported by isotopolog profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transfer of labelled FAs was not observed for the AM-specific lipid biosynthesis mutants.
source: This transfer of labelled FAs was not observed for the AM-specific lipid biosynthesis mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from isotopolog profiling experiments.

claim: Growth and development of beneficial AM fungi depends on lipid transfer from plant hosts.
source: Thus, growth and development of beneficial AM fungi is not only fueled by sugars but depends on lipid transfer from plant hosts.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data and observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) is a widespread symbiosis between most land plants and fungi of the Glomeromycota.
source: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) is a widespread symbiosis between most land plants and fungi of the Glomeromycota (Smith and Read, 2008).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: AM fungi provide mineral nutrients to the plant.
source: The fungi provide mineral nutrients to the plant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of AM fungi in the symbiosis.

claim: Nutrients are taken up from the soil and released inside root cortex cells at highly branched hyphal structures, the arbuscules.
source: These nutrients are taken up from the soil and released inside root cortex cells at highly branched hyphal structures, the arbuscules (Javot et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: AMF develop extended extraradical hyphal networks for efficient soil exploration.
source: For efficient soil exploration, arbuscular mycorrhiza fungi (AMF) develop extended extraradical hyphal networks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMF biology.

claim: Growth of AMF requires a large amount of energy and carbon building blocks, which are transported mostly as lipid droplets and glycogen to the growing hyphal tips.
source: Their growth requires a large amount of energy and carbon building blocks, which are transported mostly as lipid droplets and glycogen to the growing hyphal tips (Bago et al., 2002, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AMF are obligate biotrophs, as they depend on carbon supply by their host.
source: AMF are obligate biotrophs, as they depend on carbon supply by their host (Smith and Read, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Detailed 13C-labeled tracer-based NMR studies demonstrated that hexose sugars are a major vehicle for carbon transfer from plants to fungi.
source: In the past, detailed 13C-labeled tracer-based NMR studies demonstrated that hexose sugars are a major vehicle for carbon transfer from plants to fungi (Shachar-Hill et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A fungal hexose transporter, with high transport activity for glucose is required for arbuscule development and quantitative root colonization.
source: In addition, a fungal hexose transporter, with high transport activity for glucose is required for arbuscule development and quantitative root colonization as shown by host induced gene silencing (Helber et al., 2011), indicating the importance of hexose transfer for intra-radical fungal development.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: AMF store carbon mainly in the form of lipids.
source: AMF store carbon mainly in the form of lipids (Trépanier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The predominant storage form in AMF is triacylglycerol (TAG).
source: The predominant storage form is triacylglycerol (TAG) and the major proportion of FAs found in AMF is composed of 16:0 (palmitic acid), and of 16:1ω5 (palmitvaccenic acid).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMF lipid composition.

claim: The major proportion of FAs found in AMF is composed of 16:0 (palmitic acid), and of 16:1ω5 (palmitvaccenic acid).
source: The predominant storage form is triacylglycerol (TAG) and the major proportion of FAs found in AMF is composed of 16:0 (palmitic acid), and of 16:1ω5 (palmitvaccenic acid).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMF lipid composition.

claim: 16:1ω5 is specific to AM fungi and certain bacteria and is frequently used as marker for the detection of AM fungi in soil.
source: The latter is specific to AM fungi and certain bacteria and is frequently used as marker for the detection of AM fungi in soil (Graham et al., 1995; Bentivenga and Morton, 1996; Madan et al., 2002; Trépanier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fungus-specific 16:1ω5 FAs are not exclusive to glycerolipids but also incorporated into membrane phospholipids.
source: Fungus-specific 16:1ω5 FAs are not exclusive to glycerolipids but also incorporated into membrane phospholipids (van Aarle and Olsson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 18:1ω7 and 20:1∂11 are considered specific for AMF but do not occur in all AMF species.
source: Furthermore, 18:1ω7 and 20:1∂11 are considered specific for AMF but do not occur in all AMF species (Madan et al., 2002; Stumpe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has long been assumed that AMF use sugars as precursors for lipid biosynthesis.
source: It has long been assumed that AMF use sugars as precursors for lipid biosynthesis (Pfeffer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: De novo biosynthesis of fungal fatty acids (FAs) was only observed inside colonized roots and not in extraradical mycelia or spores.
source: However, de novo biosynthesis of fungal fatty acids (FAs) was only observed inside colonized roots and not in extraradical mycelia or spores (Pfeffer et al., 1999; Trépanier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Authors concluded that AM fungi can produce FAs only inside the host.
source: The authors concluded that AM fungi can produce FAs only inside the host.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Genes encoding multi-domain cytosolic FA synthase subunits are absent from the genomes of Rhizophagus irregularis, Gigaspora margarita and Gigaspora rosea.
source: However, recently available whole genome sequences of AMF have revealed that genes encoding multi-domain cytosolic FA synthase subunits, typically responsible for most of the de novo 16:0 FA synthesis in animals and fungi, are absent from the genomes of the model fungi Rhizophagus irregularis, Gigaspora margarita and Gigaspora rosea (Wewer et al., 2014; Ropars et al., 2016; Salvioli et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing studies.

claim: AMF appear to be unable to synthesize sufficient amounts of 16:0 FAs.
source: Hence, AMF appear to be unable to synthesize sufficient amounts of 16:0 FAs, but their genomes do encode the enzymatic machinery for 16:0 FA elongation to higher chain length and for FA desaturation (Trépanier et al., 2005; Wewer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on genome analysis data cited in the manuscript.

claim: AMF genomes encode the enzymatic machinery for 16:0 FA elongation to higher chain length and for FA desaturation.
source: Hence, AMF appear to be unable to synthesize sufficient amounts of 16:0 FAs, but their genomes do encode the enzymatic machinery for 16:0 FA elongation to higher chain length and for FA desaturation (Trépanier et al., 2005; Wewer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome analysis studies.

claim: Development of fungal arbuscules is accompanied by activation of a cohort of lipid biosynthesis genes in arbuscocytes.
source: Development of fungal arbuscules is accompanied by activation of a cohort of lipid biosynthesis genes in arbuscocytes (arbuscule-containing plant cells) (Gaude et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lipid producing plastids increase in numbers and change their position during arbuscule development.
source: Furthermore, lipid producing plastids increase in numbers and together with other organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum change their position and gather in the vicinity of the arbuscule (Lohse et al., 2005; Ivanov and Harrison, 2014), symptomatic of high metabolic activity to satisfy the high demands of arbscocytes for metabolites including lipids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Medicago truncatula mutants in AM-specific paralogs of FatM and RAM2 demonstrate the importance of plant lipid biosynthesis for arbuscule development.
source: The importance of plant lipid biosynthesis for arbuscule development has been demonstrated by Medicago truncatula mutants in AM-specific paralogs of two lipid biosynthesis genes FatM and REDUCED ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZA2 (RAM2) (Wang et al., 2012; Bravo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: FatM encodes an ACP-thioesterase, which terminates fatty acid chain elongation in the plastid.
source: FatM encodes an ACP-thioesterase, which terminates fatty acid chain elongation in the plastid by cleaving the ACP off the acyl group releasing free FAs and soluble ACP (Jones et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and established knowledge about enzyme function.

claim: RAM2 encodes a glycerol 3-phosphate acyl transferase (GPAT) and is most similar to Arabidopsis GPAT6.
source: RAM2 encodes a glycerol 3-phosphate acyl transferase (GPAT) and is most similar to Arabidopsis GPAT6.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: In Arabidopsis, GPAT6 acetylates the sn-2 position of glycerol-3-phosphate with an FA and cleaves the phosphate from lysophosphatidic acid, thereby producing sn-2-monoacylglycerol (ßMAG).
source: In Arabidopsis, GPAT6 acetylates the sn-2 position of glycerol-3-phosphate with an FA and cleaves the phosphate from lysophosphatidic acid, thereby producing sn-2-monoacylglycerol (ßMAG, Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations in both FatM and RAM2 impair arbuscule branching.
source: Mutations in both FatM and RAM2 impair arbuscule branching (Wang et al., 2012; Bravo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Arbuscule branching requires a complex of two half ABC transporters STR and STR2.
source: In addition, arbuscule branching requires a complex of two half ABC transporters STR and STR2 (Zhang et al., 2010; Gutjahr et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The substrate of STR/STR2 is unknown but other members of the ABCG transporter family are implicated in lipid transport.
source: The substrate of STR/STR2 is unknown but other members of the ABCG transporter family are implicated in lipid transport (Wittenburg and Carey, 2002; Wang et al., 2011; Fabre et al., 2016; Hwang et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It was speculated that the STR/STR2 complex may transport lipids towards arbuscules.
source: Therefore, and due to its localization in the peri-arbuscular membrane (Zhang et al., 2010) it was speculated that the STR/STR2 complex may transport lipids towards arbuscules (Gutjahr et al., 2012; Bravo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Transcriptional activation of RAM2 and STR is controlled by the GRAS transcription factor REDUCED ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZA1 (RAM1).
source: Transcriptional activation of RAM2 and STR is controlled by the GRAS transcription factor REDUCED ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZA1 (RAM1) (Gobbato et al., 2012; Park et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016) and also in ram1 mutants, arbuscule branching is impaired (Park et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In ram1 mutants, arbuscule branching is impaired.
source: Transcriptional activation of RAM2 and STR is controlled by the GRAS transcription factor REDUCED ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZA1 (RAM1) (Gobbato et al., 2012; Park et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016) and also in ram1 mutants, arbuscule branching is impaired (Park et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: RAM1, FatM, RAM2 and STR/STR2 appear to form an AM-specific operational unit for lipid biosynthesis and transport in arbuscocytes.
source: Thus, RAM1, FatM, RAM2 and STR/STR2 appear to form an AM-specific operational unit for lipid biosynthesis and transport in arbuscocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and previous research cited.

claim: RAM1, FatM, RAM2 and STR/STR2 were found to be absent from genomes of plants that have lost the ability to form AM.
source: Consistently, they were found to be absent from genomes of plants that have lost the ability to form AM (Delaux et al., 2014; Favre et al., 2014; Bravo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome analysis studies.

claim: Two Lotus japonicus mutants identified in a forward genetic screen are impaired in arbuscule branching.
source: Here, we analyzed two Lotus japonicus mutants identified in a forward genetic screen, which are impaired in arbuscule branching (Groth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation.

claim: Positional cloning combined with genome resequencing revealed mutations in a novel AM-specific β-keto-acyl ACP synthase I (KASI) gene and in the L. japonicus ortholog of M. truncatula RAM2.
source: Positional cloning combined with genome resequencing revealed mutations in a novel AM-specific β-keto-acyl ACP synthase I (KASI) gene and in the L. japonicus ortholog of M. truncatula RAM2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from genetic analysis.

claim: KASI likely acts upstream of RAM2 in producing 16:0 FAs.
source: KASI likely acts upstream of RAM2 in producing 16:0 FAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of these enzymes.

claim: The identity of the genes and the phenotypes led to the hypothesis that AMF may depend on delivery of 16:0 FAs from the plant host.
source: The identity of the genes and the phenotypes led us to hypothesize that AMF may depend on delivery of 16:0 FAs from the plant host.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and observations.

claim: Using microscopic mutant characterization, lipidomics and isotopolog profiling, the study provides strong evidence for requirement of both genes for AM-specific lipid biosynthesis and cross-kingdom lipid transfer from plants to AMF.
source: Using a combination of microscopic mutant characterization, lipidomics and isotopolog profiling of 16:0 and 16:1ω5 FAs in roots and extraradical fungal mycelium, we provide strong evidence for requirement of both genes for AM-specific lipid biosynthesis and cross-kingdom lipid transfer from plants to AMF.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dis-1 mutant (SL0154-N) and SL0181-N (red) are deficient in arbuscule branching.
source: We previously identified two L. japonicus mutants disorganized arbuscules (dis-1, SL0154-N) and SL0181-N (red) deficient in arbuscule branching (Groth et al., 2013) (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: Both dis-1 and SL0181-N mutants suffered from a reduction in root length colonization.
source: Both mutants also suffered from a reduction in root length colonization and blocked the formation of lipid-containing vesicles of the fungus Rhizophagus irregularis (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Both dis-1 and SL0181-N mutants blocked the formation of lipid-containing vesicles of Rhizophagus irregularis.
source: Both mutants also suffered from a reduction in root length colonization and blocked the formation of lipid-containing vesicles of the fungus Rhizophagus irregularis (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: DIS encodes a β-keto-acyl ACP synthase I (KASI).
source: DIS encodes a β-keto-acyl ACP synthase I (KASI, Figure 1—figure supplements 1A–C and 2).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis and sequence data.

claim: KASI enzymes catalyze successive condensation reactions during fatty acyl chain elongation from C4:0-ACP to C16:0-ACP.
source: KASI enzymes catalyze successive condensation reactions during fatty acyl chain elongation from C4:0-ACP to C16:0-ACP (Li-Beisson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KASI enzyme function, supported by a citation.

claim: SL0181-N carries one mutation (ram2-1) in the L. japonicus orthologue of Medicago truncatula RAM2.
source: SL0181-N carries one mutation (ram2-1) in the L. japonicus orthologue of the previously identified Medicago truncatula REDUCED ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZA2 (RAM2, Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis and sequence data.

claim: Arabidopsis GPAT6 has been shown to produce ß-MAG with a preference for 16:0 FAs.
source: Arabidopsis GPAT6 has been shown to produce ß-MAG with a preference for 16:0 FAs (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: DIS and RAM2 act in the same biosynthetic pathway.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that DIS and RAM2 act in the same biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known functions of the enzymes.

claim: Additional allelic dis mutants were identified by TILLING.
source: We identified additional allelic dis mutants by TILLING (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1) (Perry et al., 2003) and a ram2 mutant caused by a LORE1 insertion in the RAM2 gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) (Małolepszy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TILLING screens.

claim: A ram2 mutant was caused by a LORE1 insertion in the RAM2 gene.
source: We identified additional allelic dis mutants by TILLING (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1) (Perry et al., 2003) and a ram2 mutant caused by a LORE1 insertion in the RAM2 gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) (Małolepszy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The dis-4 mutant was chosen for further investigation because it suffers from a glycine replacement at the border of a conserved ß-sheet, which likely affects protein folding.
source: Among the allelic dis mutants we chose dis-4 for further investigation because it suffers from a glycine replacement at the border of a conserved ß-sheet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which likely affects protein folding (Perry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and a citation about mutation effects.

claim: Both allelic mutants dis-4 and ram2-2 phenocopied dis-1 and ram2-1, respectively.
source: Both allelic mutants dis-4 and ram2-2 phenocopied dis-1 and ram2-1, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Transgenic complementation of both dis-1 and ram2-1 with the wild-type versions of the mutated genes restored arbuscule-branching and wild-type-like levels of root length colonization and vesicle formation.
source: Furthermore, transgenic complementation of both dis-1 and ram2-1 with the wild-type versions of the mutated genes restored arbuscule-branching and wild-type-like levels of root length colonization and vesicle formation (Figure 1A-B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Transcript levels of both DIS and RAM2 increased in colonized roots.
source: Transcript levels of both DIS and RAM2 increased in colonized roots (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the figure.

claim: GUS activity for DIS and RAM2 promoters was predominantly detected in arbuscocytes.
source: Consistent with a role of both genes in arbuscule development GUS activity was predominantly detected in arbuscocytes (arbuscule-containing cells) in both wild-type and the corresponding mutant roots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by GUS staining data shown in figures.

claim: Nuclear localized YFP fluorescence indicated activity of both DIS and RAM2 promoters in cells containing PPAs and containing sparsely branched or mature arbuscules.
source: Nuclear localized YFP fluorescence indicated activity of both promoters in cells containing PPAs (c, Videos 1–2) and containing sparsely branched (d) or mature (e) arbuscules.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in figures and videos.

claim: YFP signal was absent from cells containing collapsed arbuscules, indicating that the promoters were active during arbuscule development and growth but inactive during arbuscule degeneration.
source: However, YFP signal was absent from cells containing collapsed arbuscules (f), indicating that the promoters were active during arbuscule development and growth but inactive during arbuscule degeneration (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in figures.

claim: RAM2 promoter activity was strictly correlated with arbuscocytes, while the DIS promoter showed additional activity in cortical cells of non-colonized root segments.
source: RAM2 promoter activity was strictly correlated with arbuscocytes, while the DIS promoter showed additional activity in cortical cells of non-colonized root segments (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D, Videos 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Arbuscocyte-specific expression of DIS and RAM2 is sufficient for fungal development.
source: To examine, whether arbuscocyte-specific expression of DIS and RAM2 is sufficient for fungal development we complemented the dis-1 and ram2-1 mutants with the corresponding wild-type genes fused to the arbuscocyte-specific PT4 promoter (Volpe et al., 2013). This restored arbuscule-branching, vesicle formation as well as root length colonization in the mutants (Figure 2C–F), showing that arbuscocyte-specific expression of DIS and RAM2 suffices to support AM development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from complementation experiments shown in figures.

claim: Expression of lipid biosynthesis genes in arbuscocytes is not only important for arbuscule branching but also for vesicle formation and quantitative colonization.
source: Thus, expression of lipid biosynthesis genes in arbuscocytes is not only important for arbuscule branching but also for vesicle formation and quantitative colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data.

claim: Growth and development of dis and ram2 mutants are not visibly affected.
source: Growth and development of dis and ram2 mutants are not visibly affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), although they carry defects in important lipid biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is supported by plant growth observations shown in the figure.

claim: RAM2 is specific to AM-competent plants.
source: RAM2 is specific to AM-competent plants (Wang et al., 2012; Delaux et al., 2014; Favre et al., 2014; Bravo et al., 2016) and activated in an AM-dependent manner (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Gobbato et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in figures.

claim: RAM2 is activated in an AM-dependent manner.
source: RAM2 is specific to AM-competent plants (Wang et al., 2012; Delaux et al., 2014; Favre et al., 2014; Bravo et al., 2016) and activated in an AM-dependent manner (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Gobbato et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in figures.

claim: Plants contain an additional GPAT6 paralog, which likely fulfills the housekeeping function.
source: Plants contain an additional GPAT6 paralog, which likely fulfills the housekeeping function (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Yang et al., 2012; Delaux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and citations.

claim: Three KASI paralogs were detected in L. japonicus: KASI, DIS and DIS-LIKE.
source: To understand whether the same applies to DIS we searched the L. japonicus genome for additional KASI genes. We detected three paralogs KASI, DIS and DIS-LIKE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), of which only DIS was transcriptionally activated in AM roots (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis and expression data.

claim: Only DIS was transcriptionally activated in AM roots among the three KASI paralogs.
source: To understand whether the same applies to DIS we searched the L. japonicus genome for additional KASI genes. We detected three paralogs KASI, DIS and DIS-LIKE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), of which only DIS was transcriptionally activated in AM roots (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the figure.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a split of seed plant KASI proteins into two different clades, called KASI and DIS.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a split of seed plant KASI proteins into two different clades, called KASI and DIS (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: Members of the KASI clade are presumably involved in housekeeping functions.
source: Members of the KASI clade, are presumably involved in housekeeping functions as this clade contains the product of the KASI single copy gene in Arabidopsis (Wu and Xue, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis and a citation.

claim: Members of the DIS clade are found specifically in AM-host dicotyledons and in a gymnosperm.
source: Members of the DIS clade are found specifically in AM-host dicotyledons and in a gymnosperm (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: DIS is absent from all eight analyzed non-host dicotyledon genomes.
source: As confirmed by synteny analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), DIS is absent from all eight analyzed non-host dicotyledon genomes, a phylogenetic pattern similar to other symbiosis genes (Delaux et al., 2014; Favre et al., 2014; Bravo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by synteny analysis data and citations.

claim: The occurrence of DIS in Lupinus species, which lost AM competence but still form root nodule symbiosis, may be a relic from the AM competent ancestor.
source: The occurrence of DIS in Lupinus species, which lost AM competence but still form root nodule symbiosis, may be a relic from the AM competent ancestor.
evidence: This is speculation based on phylogenetic patterns.

claim: A Lotus-specific duplication of the DIS gene resulted in an 87% identical copy (DIS-LIKE) located directly adjacent to DIS in a tail-to-tail orientation.
source: An apparently, Lotus-specific, and thus recent duplication of the DIS gene resulted in an 87% identical copy (DIS-LIKE) located directly adjacent to DIS in a tail-to-tail orientation (Figure 1—figure supplements 1B–C, 2).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis data.

claim: DIS-LIKE was expressed at very low levels and not induced upon AM.
source: DIS-LIKE was expressed at very low levels and not induced upon AM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the figure.

claim: In roots of dis-like-5, AM and arbuscule development was indistinguishable from wild type.
source: However, in roots of dis-like-5 AM and arbuscule development was indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: DIS-LIKE might have lost its major role in arbuscule development after the duplication.
source: Therefore, DIS-LIKE might have lost its major role in arbuscule development after the duplication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotype and expression data.

claim: DIS was exclusively found in genomes of AM-competent dicotyledons and a gymnosperm.
source: Interestingly, DIS was exclusively found in genomes of AM-competent dicotyledons and a gymnosperm (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: DIS has been lost at the split of the mono- from dicotyledons.
source: This implies that DIS has been lost at the split of the mono- from dicotyledons.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: DIS and the single copy housekeeping KASI gene of Arabidopsis are interchangeable.
source: Despite the phylogenetic divergence, DIS and the single copy housekeeping KASI gene of Arabidopsis are interchangeable (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by cross-species complementation data shown in the figure.

claim: The specificity of DIS to function in AM symbiosis is probably encoded in its promoter.
source: Therefore, the specificity of DIS to function in AM symbiosis is probably encoded in its promoter (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data and promoter activity data.

claim: In monocotyledons, the promoter of the housekeeping KASI gene may have acquired additional regulatory elements, sufficient for arbuscocyte-specific activation, thus making DIS dispensable.
source: In monocotyledons, the promoter of the housekeeping KASI gene may have acquired additional regulatory elements, sufficient for arbuscocyte-specific activation, thus making DIS dispensable.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phylogenetic pattern and functional data.

claim: AMF were unable to incorporate 13C into FAs when fed with [U-13C6]glucose in absence of the host plant.
source: This showed that: (1) AMF were unable to incorporate 13C into FAs when fed with [U-13C6]glucose in absence of the host plant.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: When associated with a wild-type host, the fungal extraradical mycelium accumulated 13C labelled 16:0 FAs and the isotopolog profile of these 16:0 FAs was almost identical with the host profile.
source: (2) When associated with a wild-type host, the fungal extraradical mycelium accumulated 13C labelled 16:0 FAs and the isotopolog profile of these 16:0 FAs was almost identical with the host profile.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: The 16:0 FA isotopolog fingerprint differed strongly between two different wild-type plant systems (Lotus seedling and carrot hairy root) but for each of them the fungal mycelium recapitulated the isotopolog profile.
source: (3) The 16:0 FA isotopolog fingerprint differed strongly between two different wild-type plant systems (Lotus seedling and carrot hairy root) but for each of them the fungal mycelium recapitulated the isotopolog profile.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: The plant dominates the isotopolog profile of the fungus.
source: Therefore clearly, the plant dominates the profile of the fungus, because it is impossible that the fungus by itself generates the same FA isotopolog pattern as the plant – especially in the absence of cytosolic FA synthase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the isotopolog profiling data and the absence of fungal FA synthase genes.

claim: The isotopolog profile of fungus-specific 16:1 ω5 FAs inside and outside the root resembled the plant 16:0 FA profile.
source: (4) In agreement, the isotopolog profile of fungus-specific 16:1 ω5 FAs inside and outside the root also resembled the plant 16:0 FA profile.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: Colonized dis and ram2 mutant roots resembled the 16:0 FA isotopolog profile of L. japonicus wild-type roots.
source: (5) Colonized dis and ram2 mutant roots resembled the 16:0 FA isotopolog profile of L. japonicus wild-type roots.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: The 16:0 FA profile of the fungal extraradical mycelium and the 16:1ω5 FA profile inside the roots showed a very different pattern in mutants, consistent with very low transport of labelled FAs to the fungus when associated with the mutants.
source: However, the 16:0 FA profile of the fungal extraradical mycelium and the 16:1ω5 FA profile inside the roots showed a very different pattern, consistent with very low transport of labelled FAs to the fungus when associated with the mutants.
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data.

claim: DIS and RAM2 are specifically required for the synthesis of 16:0 ß-MAG.
source: (6) DIS and RAM2 are specifically required for the synthesis of 16:0 ß-MAG (Figure 7) and the predominant FA chain length found in AM fungi is precisely 16.
evidence: This is supported by MAG quantification data shown in the figure.

claim: The predominant FA chain length found in AM fungi is precisely 16.
source: (6) DIS and RAM2 are specifically required for the synthesis of 16:0 ß-MAG (Figure 7) and the predominant FA chain length found in AM fungi is precisely 16.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMF lipid composition.

claim: dis and ram2 roots do not allow the formation of lipid-containing fungal vesicles and accumulate very low levels of fungal signature lipids.
source: (7) dis and ram2 roots do not allow the formation of lipid-containing fungal vesicles and accumulate very low levels of fungal signature lipids (Figure 5 and figure supplements).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in figures.

claim: DIS and RAM2 are required to provide lipids for transfer to the fungus.
source: Together this strongly supports the idea that DIS and RAM2 are required to provide lipids for transfer to the fungus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from mutant analysis, lipidomics, and isotopolog profiling.

claim: In the mutants, the fungus is deprived of lipids.
source: Consequently, in the mutants, the fungus is deprived of lipids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes and lipid analysis.

claim: The promoters of DIS and RAM2 are active in arbusocytes and already during PPA formation, the earliest visible stage of arbuscocyte development.
source: The promoters of DIS and RAM2 are active in arbusocytes and already during PPA formation, the earliest visible stage of arbuscocyte development.
evidence: This is supported by promoter activity data shown in figures.

claim: Plant lipids are needed for arbuscule growth, probably to provide material for the extensive plasma-membrane of the highly branched fungal structure.
source: Together with the stunted arbuscule phenotype of dis, ram2 and fatm mutants (Figure 1 [Bravo et al., 2017]) this suggests that plant lipids are needed for arbuscule growth, probably to provide material for the extensive plasma-membrane of the highly branched fungal structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes and the known structure of arbuscules.

claim: The arbuscule dictates development of the AMF as a whole, since lipid uptake at the arbuscule is required for vesicle formation, full exploration of the root and development of extraradical mycelia and spores.
source: It also indicates that the arbuscule dictates development of the AMF as a whole, since lipid uptake at the arbuscule is required for vesicle formation, full exploration of the root and development of extraradical mycelia and spores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes showing reduced vesicle formation and colonization.

claim: Defective arbuscule development was also observed for the phylogenetically distantly related AMF Gigaspora rosea.
source: Defective arbuscule development was also observed for the different and phylogenetically distantly related AMF Gigaspora rosea (Groth et al., 2013), which similar to R. irregularis lacks genes encoding cytosolic FA synthase from their genomes (Wewer et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dependence on plant lipids delivered at the arbuscule is likely a common phenomenon among AMF and a hallmark of AMF obligate biotrophy.
source: Hence the dependence on plant lipids delivered at the arbuscule is likely a common phenomenon among AMF and a hallmark of AMF obligate biotrophy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple AMF species lack FA synthase genes.

claim: The fungus can initially colonize the mutant roots with a low amount of intraradical hyphae and stunted arbuscules.
source: Despite the obvious central importance of lipid uptake by the arbuscule, the fungus can initially colonize the mutant roots with a low amount of intraradical hyphae and stunted arbuscules (Figure 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by colonization data shown in figures.

claim: The construction of membranes for initial colonization may be supported by the large amounts of lipids stored in AMF spores.
source: The construction of membranes for this initial colonization may be supported by the large amounts of lipids stored in AMF spores.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of initial colonization in mutants.

claim: It is possible that plant housekeeping enzymes provide lipids to intraradical hyphae before arbuscule formation.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that plant housekeeping enzymes provide lipids to intraradical hyphae before arbuscule formation.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Activity of the housekeeping KASI may be responsible for slightly higher colonization levels observed for dis in some experiments as compared to other mutants.
source: Activity of the housekeeping KASI may also be responsible for slightly higher colonization levels observed for dis in some experiments as compared to other mutants.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed differences in colonization levels.

claim: Photosynthetic wild-type nurse plants can restore arbuscule-branching in Medicago ram2 and str mutants.
source: It has recently been reported that photosynthetic wild-type nurse plants can restore arbuscule-branching in Medicago ram2 and str mutants (Jiang et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017), suggesting that lipids can be supplied to arbuscules via the extraradical hyphal network and intraradical hyphae through this route support arbuscule fine-branching.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Lipids need to be provided cell-autonomously by the arbuscocyte to support arbuscule fine-branching.
source: Based on four observations, we favor an alternative szenario, in which lipids need to be provided cell-autonomously by the arbuscocyte to support arbuscule fine-branching.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Presence of nurse carrot hairy roots did not restore arbuscule branching in dis, ram2 and str.
source: (1) Presence of nurse carrot hairy roots did not restore arbuscule branching in dis, ram2 and str (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: dis and ram2 were found in a forward genetics screen based on their stunted arbuscule phenotype, where the fungal inoculum was provided via chive nurse plants.
source: (2) dis and ram2 were found in a forward genetics screen based on their stunted arbuscule phenotype. In this screen, the fungal inoculum was provided via chive nurse plants (Groth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original screen.

claim: Map-based cloning of Lotus dis, ram2 and str was performed with segregating mutant populations grown in the same pot, in which the wild-type and heterozygeous siblings acted as nurse plants on the homozygeous mutants, and the stunted arbuscule phenotype was easily observable.
source: (3) Map-based cloning of Lotus dis, ram2 and str (Kojima et al., 2014) was performed with segregating mutant populations grown in the same pot, in which the wild-type and heterozygeous siblings acted as nurse plants on the homozygeous mutants. In this system, the stunted arbuscule phenotype was easily observable.
evidence: This is based on the methods used in the study.

claim: Arbuscule branching in a rice str mutant was not restored by wild type nurse plants.
source: (4) Arbuscule branching in a rice str mutant was not restored by wild type nurse plants (Gutjahr et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RAM2 is the most downstream acting enzyme in arbuscocyte-specific lipid biosynthesis known to date.
source: RAM2 is the most downstream acting enzyme in arbuscocyte-specific lipid biosynthesis known to date (Figure 9).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known pathway and the data presented.

claim: RAM2 is predicted to synthesize ß-MAG.
source: It is predicted to synthesize ß-MAG and we and others have shown that 16:0 ß-MAGs are indeed reduced in colonized roots of dis, fatm and ram2 mutants, providing evidence that this is likely the case (Figure 7, [Bravo et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: 16:0 ß-MAGs are reduced in colonized roots of dis, fatm and ram2 mutants.
source: It is predicted to synthesize ß-MAG and we and others have shown that 16:0 ß-MAGs are indeed reduced in colonized roots of dis, fatm and ram2 mutants, providing evidence that this is likely the case (Figure 7, [Bravo et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and citations.

claim: 16:0 ß-MAG as transport vehicle for 16:0 FAs to the fungus is a good candidate because it has certain advantages.
source: Although, we cannot exclude that a downstream metabolite of 16:0 ß-MAG is transported to the fungus, 16:0 ß-MAG as transport vehicle for 16:0 FAs to the fungus is a good candidate because conceptually this molecule may bear certain advantages.
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of ß-MAG.

claim: ß-MAGs are not used for plant storage or membrane lipid biosynthesis but rather as pre-cursors for cuticle formation in Arabidopsis.
source: It has been shown in Arabidopsis that ß-MAGs are not used for plant storage or membrane lipid biosynthesis but rather as pre-cursors for cuticle formation (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The production of ß-MAGs could be a way to withdraw FAs from the plants own metabolism to make them available to the fungus.
source: The production of ß-MAGs could therefore, be a way, to withdraw FAs from the plants own metabolism to make them available to the fungus.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of ß-MAG production.

claim: ß-MAGs are small and amphiphilic and could diffuse across the short distance of the hydrophilic apoplastic space between plant and fungal membrane.
source: In addition, ß-MAGs are small and amphiphilic and could diffuse across the short distance of the hydrophilic apoplastic space between plant and fungal membrane.
evidence: This is speculation based on the chemical properties of ß-MAG.

claim: At the newly growing arbuscule branches the distance between the plant and fungal membrane is very small and has been measured to be 80–100 nm on TEM images.
source: At the newly growing arbuscule branches the distance between the plant and fungal membrane is indeed very small and has been measured to be 80–100 nm on TEM images of high-pressure freeze-substituted samples (Bonfante, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fungus-specific 16:1ω5 ß-MAGs could not be detected in colonized roots.
source: However, we could not detect fungus-specific 16:1ω5 ß-MAGs in colonized roots.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The fungus may metabolize ß-MAGs before desaturation of the 16:0 FAs to synthesize membrane and storage lipids.
source: This could mean that the fungus metabolizes them before desaturation of the 16:0 FAs to synthesize membrane and storage lipids.
evidence: This is speculation about fungal metabolism.

claim: ß-MAGs may not be taken up by the fungus.
source: Alternatively, ß-MAGs may not be taken up by the fungus.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative scenarios.

claim: ß-MAGs are known to isomerize to α-MAGs in acid or basic conditions.
source: ß-MAGs are known to isomerize to α-MAGs in acid or basic conditions (Iqbal and Hussain, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that ß-MAGs isomerize in the acidic periarbuscular space before being taken up by the arbuscule.
source: It is therefore, possible that they isomerize in the acidic periarbuscular space (Guttenberger, 2000) before being taken up by the arbuscule.
evidence: This is speculation based on the chemical properties of ß-MAG and the pH of the periarbuscular space.

claim: Good candidates for MAG transporters are the ABCG half transporters STR and STR2.
source: How are MAGs transported across the peri-arbuscular membrane? Good candidates for MAG transporters are the ABCG half transporters STR and STR2.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of similar transporters.

claim: Similar ABCG transporters have been implicated genetically in cuticle formation, which also requires ß-MAGs.
source: Similar ABCG transporters have been implicated genetically in cuticle formation, which also requires ß-MAGs (Pighin et al., 2004; Panikashvili et al., 2011; Yeats et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The half ABCG transporters STR and STR2 are both independently required for arbuscule branching and they need to interact to form a full transporter.
source: The half ABCG transporters STR and STR2 are both independently required for arbuscule branching and they need to interact to form a full transporter (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Colonized roots of a L. japonicus str mutant did not allow the formation of fungal vesicles and had the same lipid profile as dis and ram2.
source: We found that colonized roots of a L. japonicus str mutant, did not allow the formation of fungal vesicles and had the same lipid profile as dis and ram2 (Figure 5 and figure supplements).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The 13C labelling experiment demonstrated that str mutants do not transfer lipids to the fungus.
source: Furthermore, our 13C labelling experiment demonstrated that str mutants do not transfer lipids to the fungus (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by isotopolog profiling data shown in the figure.

claim: Strong evidence for the role of STR in lipid transport across the periarbuscular membrane is still lacking and the substrate of STR remains to be determined.
source: Although these are encouraging indications, strong evidence for the role of STR in lipid transport across the periarbuscular membrane is still lacking and the substrate of STR remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current data.

claim: It cannot be excluded that mutation of str has an indirect effect on lipid transport.
source: Therefore, currently, it cannot be excluded that mutation of str has an indirect effect on lipid transport and alternative mechanisms for example lipid translocation via vesicle fission and fusion are possible.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Several ABC transporter genes are expressed in planta in AMF.
source: Nevertheless, also in AMF, several ABC transporter genes are expressed in planta (Tisserant et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If lipid transport via ABC transporters would play a role, some of the fungal ABC transporters could be involved in uptake of lipids into the fungal cytoplasm.
source: They are not characterized, but if lipid transport via ABC transporters instead of other mechanisms would play a role, some of them could be involved in uptake of lipids into the fungal cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculation about potential fungal mechanisms.

claim: Mutants in the GRAS gene RAM1 are impaired in AM-specific lipid accumulation in colonized roots.
source: We found that mutants in the GRAS gene RAM1 are impaired in AM-specific lipid accumulation in colonized roots and in AM-mediated activation of DIS and the single copy gene KASIII (Figure 6), in addition to FatM, RAM2 and STR (Wang et al., 2012; Park et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and citations.

claim: ram1 mutants are impaired in AM-mediated activation of DIS and the single copy gene KASIII.
source: We found that mutants in the GRAS gene RAM1 are impaired in AM-specific lipid accumulation in colonized roots and in AM-mediated activation of DIS and the single copy gene KASIII (Figure 6), in addition to FatM, RAM2 and STR (Wang et al., 2012; Park et al., 2015; Pimprikar et al., 2016; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the figure.

claim: Plants have evolved an AM-specific regulatory module for lipid production in arbuscocytes and delivery to the fungus.
source: This suggests that plants have evolved an AM-specific regulatory module for lipid production in arbuscocytes and delivery to the fungus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the regulatory role of RAM1 and the coordinated expression of lipid biosynthesis genes.

claim: The finding that plants transfer lipids to AMF completely changes the previous view that the fungus receives only sugars from the plant.
source: Our finding that plants transfer lipids to AMF completely changes the previous view that the fungus receives only sugars from the plant (Pfeffer et al., 1999; Trépanier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented and citations to previous views.

claim: It will be interesting to determine the relative contributions of sugar and lipid transfer to AMF, and whether this may be a determinant of variation in root length colonization and extraradical mycelium formation depending on the plant-fungal genotype combination.
source: It will now be interesting to determine the relative contributions of sugar and lipid transfer to AMF, and whether this may be a determinant of variation in root length colonization and extraradical mycelium formation depending on the plant-fungal genotype combination (Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: It is conceivable that supply of plant lipids to the fungus plus fungal lipid transport is more energy efficient for the symbiosis as a whole than fungal carbohydrate transport plus fungal lipid biosynthesis.
source: FA biosynthesis consumes more energy than biosynthesis of carbohydrates and organic carbon provided by the plant needs to be transported in fungal hyphae over long distances from the inside of the root to the extremities of the extraradical mycelium. Therefore, it is conceivable that supply of plant lipids to the fungus plus fungal lipid transport is more energy efficient for the symbiosis as a whole than fungal carbohydrate transport plus fungal lipid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on energetic considerations.

claim: Inter-organismic lipid transfer followed by loss of fungal FA biosynthesis genes may have been selected for during evolution because it likely optimized the symbiosis for most rapid proliferation of extraradical mycelium.
source: Hence, inter-organismic lipid transfer followed by loss of fungal FA biosynthesis genes may have been selected for during evolution because it likely optimized the symbiosis for most rapid proliferation of extraradical mycelium, thus ensuring efficient mineral nutrient acquisition from the soil for supporting the plant host.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary selection.

claim: Lipid transfer across kingdoms has also been observed in human parasites or symbiotic bacteria of insects.
source: Lipid transfer across kingdoms has also been observed in human parasites or symbiotic bacteria of insects (Caffaro and Boothroyd, 2011; Elwell et al., 2011; Herren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It will be interesting to learn whether lipid transfer is a more widespread phenomenon among biotrophic inter-organismic interactions.
source: It will be interesting to learn whether this is a more widespread phenomenon among biotrophic inter-organismic interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader significance of the findings.
